![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187947/assets/f504ea91bae5d27b3e7b31d697ed06c9e34d838724e8dafac46e69d84de9c3cf.png)

A gas station has a rectangular gasoline storage tank stored underground. The tank is $15\text{ feet}$ long and $10\text{ feet}$ wide. A worker lowers a dip stick into the tank and notices that the depth of the gasoline is decreasing by $2\text{ feet}$ every hour. How fast is the volume of gasoline decreasing?
question.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the gasoline in the tank, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=15\,\text{ft},\,W=10\,\text{ft},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-2\,\text{ft}/\text{hour}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of the gasoline in the tank:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(15)(10)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =150\cdot (-2) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gasoline level is decreasing at a rate of $300\,{\text{ft}}^{3}\text{/hour}.$
